en: Title: *Dharmadhātustava* Author: Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna Source: Liu 2015, implementing corrections in Kano 2015
Homage to you, O Dharmadhātu, who abide within all sentient beings!

Because they do not fully understand you, they wander in the abode of the three realms of existence. That very same element which is being purified within saṃsāra is indeed that very same thing when pure in nirvāṇa; for it is truly the Dharmakāya.
Just as the cream of ghee mixed with milk is not seen,
so too the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) mixed with afflictions is not seen.
Just as milk, when purified, becomes the substance of ghee that is perfectly stainless.
In this way, when the afflictions are purified, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) becomes perfectly stainless.
Just as a lamp situated within a jar does not illuminate anything at all, so too the realm of phenomena, situated within the jar of the afflictions, does not shine forth.
For from whichever side that jar has a hole,
from that very side its rays have issued forth.
When that jar is shattered by the vajra of meditative concentration, [the rays no longer escape].<6>
It shines forth everywhere, extending as far as space.
The realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is never arisen nor ever ceased;
it is at all times undefiled, pure in its beginning, middle, and end.

Just as a lapis lazuli gem, though radiant at all times, does not have its luster shine when concealed within a covering of stone; even so, the utterly stainless realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), when shrouded by afflictions, does not manifest. <9>
He does not shine in saṃsāra, but in nirvāṇa he is luminous. (10) When the lineage exists, there is exertion, as shown by the example of gold;
when the lineage does not exist, exertion is held to be nothing but weariness. (11)
For just as grain covered by husks is not considered to be its actual fruit,
so too one who is shrouded by afflictions is not conceived of as a Buddha. For just as that same fruit appears once it is freed from the husks, [so does he appear when free from afflictions].
For thus it is that the Dharma-body, liberated from afflictions, shines forth.
An analogy is made in the world by means of the plantain tree, which has no core;
yet its fruits possess a core and are consumed as if they were like nectar.
Thus, in this essence-less saṃsāra, when the ocean of afflictions has been stilled,
even for him the fruit is Buddhahood— the nectar for all embodied beings.
For indeed, from all seeds, a corresponding fruit is produced.
Without seeds there is no fruit; what wise person would accept this?
But this element, being the seed of all phenomena, is considered their basis;
when purified in this gradual manner, it brings about the state of Buddhahood.
For the stainless sun and moon are indeed obscured by five impurities:
by clouds, mist, smoke, the mouth of Rāhu, dust, and so forth.
In this same way, the luminous mind is obscured by five impurities.
Through sensual desire, ill will, sloth, restlessness, and doubt—
just as a garment soiled with various stains may be purified by fire,
yet when cast into the midst of the fire, the stains are consumed but not the nature of the cloth. (19–20)
Thus, the mind, which is luminous by nature, is defiled by stains born of passion;
yet when those stains are consumed by the fire of gnosis, that luminosity itself is not burned.
Whatever sūtras were spoken by the Victors that provide nourishment for emptiness—
Through all of these, there is the turning away of the afflictions, but not the destruction of the element.
Just as water hidden within the earth remains pure,
so too does gnosis shine forth perfectly pure when it is concealed by the afflictions.

Since the *dharmadhātu* is neither self nor female, male, or neuter, and is entirely free from all grasping, how can it be conceptualized as a "self"? For all phenomena are indeed unattached; for them, femininity and masculinity do not exist.
Indeed, the state of being male or female was demonstrated for the sake of disciplining those blinded by passion.
There are three mental realizations: that things are impermanent, suffering, and empty;
the supreme mental realization is the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena.
Just as an embryo exists within a pregnant woman yet is not seen,
so too the reality of phenomena (dharmatattva), shrouded by afflictions, is not seen.
Indeed, the arising of the four types of conceptual construction occurs from the primary elements and their derivatives.
For the conceptual construction of "I" and "mine" arises from names, designations, and signs.
Indeed, the vow of the Buddhas is without appearance and without characteristics;
because it is to be personally realized by yogins, it is the eternal nature of the Buddhas.
Just as a hare's horn does not exist even when it is conceptualized,
so too among all phenomena that which is conceptualized does not exist at all. Yet, while a single atom may exist, a cow's horn does not exist.
As it was before, so it is after; what can be conceived of that by the Buddhas?
It arises in dependence and ceases in dependence;
there is no occurrence of a single entity—how is it conceptualized by the foolish?
Both the examples of the hare’s horn and the cow’s horn are characterized by conceptual construction;
one should attain the Middle Way according to the true nature of the Sugata’s Dharma, just as [the reflection of] the moon, sun, and stars appears in a clear vessel of water. <33>
For a reflection is seen; likewise is the perfected characteristic (niṣpannalakṣaṇa).
It is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end, non-deceptive, and eternal.
Since no such self exists therein, how can it be imagined as a "self"?
Just as water is called "hot" during the summer season, yet that very same water is called "cold" during the winter seasons; so too,
when enveloped by the web of afflictions, the mind is so designated.
That very [nature], through the departure of afflictions, is designated as "Buddha.
<37> Depending upon the eye and forms, and with utterly pure illuminations, those which are unarisen and unceasing perceive the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). <38>
Depending on the ear and sound, the mind and the three types of representation perceive the signless realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) through their own conceptual construction.
Relying on the nose and odor, one smells that which is formless and invisible.
The suchness of olfactory consciousness is conceptualized as the dharma-realm.
(40) For the tongue is empty of intrinsic nature; it is the seclusion of the taste-realm.
Non-abiding consciousness is the very nature of the dharma-realm. (41)
I declare that the *dharmadhātu* is by nature the pure body, characterized by the condition of contact, yet liberated from all conditions;
it is free from the imagined and the imagining within the phenomena dominated by the mind.
The absence of intrinsic nature in phenomena is discerned as the *dharmadhātu*.
The yogi sees, hears, smells, tastes, touches, and likewise cognizes phenomena; such is the characteristic of the perfected (*niṣpanna*).
The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and likewise the mind—the purification of these six sense bases is the characteristic of reality.
This mind is seen to be twofold: that which is mundane and that which is supramundane.
Through the grasping at a self comes saṃsāra, for that [grasping] is the suchness of each individual.
Nirvāṇa is indeed the destruction of passion, as well as the destruction of hatred and delusion;
through the awakening to that, Buddhahood is the refuge for all embodied beings.
Within this physical body, all that is knowledge and even ignorance is bound by one's own conceptual construction and liberated through thorough self-cognition.
Awakening is neither distant nor near; it has neither gone nor come.
It is neither seen nor indeed not seen right here within this cage of afflictions.
And it is said in the collections of sūtras: "The one who contemplates the self dwells by means of the dwelling of the lamp of wisdom, having attained supreme peace."
One should not have the notion that awakening is distant, nor should one have the notion that it is near; for,
through the thorough knowledge of the six sense objects as they truly appear,
it is like milk mixed with water in a single vessel.
For swans drink the milk while the water remains as it is; likewise,
yogins drink the knowledge that is mixed with afflictions within the single vessel,
while they cast aside what is not knowledge.
As long as the external world is conceptualized through the grasping of "I" or "mine," so long does the seed of existence persist.
But when the selflessness of objects is perceived, the seed of existence is extinguished.
For the Buddha enters final nirvāṇa—he is pure, eternal, and the abode of auspiciousness.
Fools conceptualize duality, whereas non-duality is the state of yogins.

Through various difficult acts of giving, through ethical discipline, through gathering beings for their welfare, and through patience that assists sentient beings— this nourishment of the element (dhātu) is threefold.
Vigor in all dharmas, the mind directed toward meditative concentration,
and being eternally unshakable in wisdom— this, moreover, is the nourishment of awakening.
Wisdom conjoined with skillful means and purified by aspirational prayers.
Knowledge is well-established in the powers, and the nourishment of the elements is fourfold.
Do not pay homage to the Bodhisattvas; this was a very ill-spoken [statement].
Regarding the Bodhisattva who is without life... [the rest of the verse is missing].
Having placed [the materials] here, one should contemplate;
there, the production of jaggery, sugar, and candied sugar occurs.
When the bodhicitta has been protected, one should reflect upon it here with focused attention;
therein arises the birth of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas.
Just as farmers provide protection for rice seedlings and the like, so too should one guard this mind.
Likewise, the Leaders provide protection for those who have faith in their own basis.
Just as the form of the moon is seen on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
so too is the form of the Buddha seen by those who have faith in the Supreme Vehicle.
Just as the growth of the new moon is seen moment by moment,
so too is the growth of those who have entered the stages seen moment by moment.
For just as on the fifteenth day, indeed, the full moon comes into being.
Thus, on the stage of ultimate attainment, the Dharma-body indeed arises.
For one whose resolve regarding the Buddha and the Dharma is firm at all times,
that irreversible mind is generated in birth after birth.
The transformation of the basis that was dark and the acquisition of the basis that is bright—
through the awakening to that [reality] at that time, it is called "Joy" (muditā).
For [the mind] has always been defiled by various impurities such as passion and the like.

The purity that exists when stains are absent is designated as "Stainless" (vimalā). Because the web of afflictions has been ceased, it is "Radiant" (prabhākarī), being brilliantly pure and free from the immeasurable darkness. <69–70>
Pure, eternally luminous, and forever free from attachments,
surrounded by the flames of gnosis, this stage is considered Arciṣmatī (The Radiant).
[71] It possesses the manifold variety of all sciences, arts, crafts, and meditations.

For the victory over the afflictions that are difficult to conquer is indeed very hard to achieve. This stage, which is profound in its arising and passing away, encompasses all perfections and constitutes the three types of enlightenment; it is the stage called "The Manifest" (Abhimukhī).
It sports with a web of rays and circular arrays on all sides;
having crossed the flood of mud from the three worlds, it is known as "Far-reaching" (dūraṅgamā). Sustained by the Buddhas, it has entered the ocean of gnosis.
Having attained mastery over effortlessness, he is unshakable by the servants of Māra.
Having reached the further shore in all the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), that yogi,
through his teaching of the Dharma and his discourses, is known as being on the stage of "Excellent Intelligence" (*sādhumatī*).
The Cloud of Dharma of the Buddhas sustains everywhere their delightful body composed of gnosis, which is as stainless as space;
it is the support of all dharmas and the encompassing of the fruits of spiritual practice.
The transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) is designated as the *dharmakāya*.
It is inconceivable when free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), yet it is conceivable when characterized by the impressions of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
You are inconceivable to all; who is worthy of knowing you?
Beyond the scope of all speech, outside the range of all the senses,
you are accessible only to the mental consciousness— whatever you are, whatever you are, homage be to you!
<80> Thus have the sons of the Buddha, of great renown, been gradually brought forth.
Through the knowledge of the Cloud of Dharma, they perceive the emptiness of the true nature of phenomena.
When the mind has been purified and has crossed over the ocean of existence,
its seat, consisting of a great lotus, becomes firmly established.
Resplendent with the luster of many jewel-leaves, radiant with the marks of excellence,
and surrounded on all sides by many tens of millions of lotuses,
the Child remains like the young moon, endowed with the ten powers.
Those whose beings are defiled by afflictions do not see the Tathāgata.
Just as hungry ghosts see the ocean everywhere as dry,
so too for those consumed by ignorance there is the conceptualization that "the Buddha does not exist."
What will the Blessed One do for sentient beings of little merit? [Regarding their] birth... [text missing]. || <86>
